steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing a new iterative method (based on alternating projection) for training and inference in large-scale Gaussian processes. Motivate it against existing scalable GP approaches and conjugate gradients, and end with a short contributions subsection summarizing the method, the theory and the empirical results.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Scaling Gaussian process (GP) models to large datasets has been a central research topic in probabilistic machine learning for nearly two decades. The main challenge is the cubic complexity of computing the marginal log likelihood (MLL) during training and also the predictive distribution at test time. Over the years people have addressed this problem from a modeling perspective and from a numerical methods perspective, and contemporary work even unifies the two perspectives to some degree. Recently, numerical methods have relied more and more on matrix-free iterative methods, which access the kernel matrix through matrix-vector multiplications. These iterations are suitable for GPU acceleration and they have been successful on medium to moderately large datasets, where they outperform modeling-based approaches like stochastic variational GPs (SVGP).

Most GP training and inference approaches that are based on iterative methods use classic general-purpose algorithms for matrix solves, such as conjugate gradients (CG), MINRES, or (stochastic) gradient descent. There is reason to think these algorithms are suboptimal for modern hardware-accelerated Gaussian processes. For example, CG was built specifically for sparse linear systems that need high-precision solutions. Neither of these properties applies to GP regression. The solves we need involve dense covariance matrices, and tasks like hyperparameter optimization can be done with extremely coarse-grained solves. Large-scale dense operations and being fine with low precision are in line with existing trends in machine learning, but in the end they put Gaussian processes at odds with a lot of the literature on numerical methods.

- Goal: like purpose-built optimizers in deep learning, a purpose-built method for (coarse-grained) covariance solves on modern hardware
  - iterative method for gradients of MLL and posterior mean
  - vs CG: 1) \mathcal{O}(n) per iteration vs \mathcal{O}(n^{2}); 2) fast monotone early convergence (not necessarily higher precision); 3) better numerical stability in floating point

## Contributions.

- MLL derivative + posterior mean via alternating projection
- iteration uses subblock of kernel matrix, linear time/memory, residual decreases near-monotonically per epoch
- linear convergence, no slower than gradient descent
- up to 27\times (training) and 72\times (inference) speed-up over CG
- 4 million data points without inducing points; beats SVGP by significant margin

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Scaling Gaussian process (GP) models to large datasets has been a central research topic in probabilistic machine learning for nearly two decades. The main challenge is the cubic complexity of computing the marginal log likelihood (MLL) during training and also the predictive distribution at test time. Over the years people have addressed this problem from a modeling perspective and from a numerical methods perspective, and contemporary work even unifies the two perspectives to some degree. Recently, numerical methods have relied more and more on matrix-free iterative methods, which access the kernel matrix through matrix-vector multiplications. These iterations are suitable for GPU acceleration and they have been successful on medium to moderately large datasets, where they outperform modeling-based approaches like stochastic variational GPs (SVGP).

Most GP training and inference approaches that are based on iterative methods use classic general-purpose algorithms for matrix solves, such as conjugate gradients (CG), MINRES, or (stochastic) gradient descent. There is reason to think these algorithms are suboptimal for modern hardware-accelerated Gaussian processes. For example, CG was built specifically for sparse linear systems that need high-precision solutions. Neither of these properties applies to GP regression. The solves we need involve dense covariance matrices, and tasks like hyperparameter optimization can be done with extremely coarse-grained solves. Large-scale dense operations and being fine with low precision are in line with existing trends in machine learning, but in the end they put Gaussian processes at odds with a lot of the literature on numerical methods.

Deep learning has been revolutionized by purpose-built optimizers that exploit properties of neural networks, and in the same way this paper aims to accelerate GPs with a purpose-built method that leverages (coarse-grained) covariance matrix solves on modern hardware. We introduce an iterative method to compute gradients of the marginal log-likelihood (MLL) and the posterior mean. It improves over CG in these ways: 1) it needs \mathcal{O}(n) computation per iteration instead of CG's \mathcal{O}(n^{2}); 2) it converges rapidly and monotonically in its early stages (but it does not necessarily get higher precision than CG); and 3) it has improved numerical stability in floating point arithmetic.

## Contributions.

We propose an iterative method for Gaussian process training and inference. It computes the marginal log-likelihood derivative and the posterior mean via alternating projection. Each iteration of the algorithm accesses a subblock of the kernel matrix and has linear time and memory complexity, and the residual decreases near-monotonically after every epoch. We prove that the algorithm converges linearly at a rate no slower than gradient descent, even though it never operates on the full kernel matrix. Empirically, our method gets a speed-up of up to 27\times over CG-based hyperparameter training and up to 72\times over CG-based inference on a wide range of datasets. To show its scalability and robustness to ill-conditioning, we train Gaussian processes on 4 million data points, which to the best of our knowledge is the largest dataset reported in the literature to-date without using inducing points or similar modeling approximations. Our method outperforms the stochastic variational Gaussian process by a significant margin at this scale.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Scaling Gaussian process (GP) models to large datasets has been a central research topic in probabilistic machine learning for nearly two decades. The primary challenge is the cubic complexity of computing both the marginal log likelihood (MLL) during training and the predictive distribution at test time. Over the years, this problem has been addressed both from a modeling perspective [1,2,3,4,5,6,7] and from a numerical methods perspective [8,9,10,11,12], and contemporary work even unifies these perspectives to a degree [13,14]. In recent years, numerical methods have increasingly relied on matrix-free iterative methods, which access the kernel matrix through matrix-vector multiplications. These iterations are suitable for GPU acceleration [10] and have been successful on medium to moderately large datasets [11], outperforming modeling-based approaches such as stochastic variational GPs (SVGP) [1].

Most GP training and inference approaches based on iterative methods use classic general-purpose algorithms for matrix solves, such as conjugate gradients (CG) [8,10,11], MINRES [15], or (stochastic) gradient descent [16]. There is reason to believe that such algorithms are suboptimal for modern hardware-accelerated Gaussian processes. For example, CG was purpose-built for sparse linear systems that require high-precision solutions. Neither of these properties applies to GP regression: the necessary solves involve dense covariance matrices, and tasks such as hyperparameter optimization can be performed with extremely coarse-grained solves [11,12]. These characteristics of large-scale dense operations and amenability to low precision are in line with existing trends in machine learning [17,18], but they ultimately place Gaussian processes at odds with much of the numerical methods literature.

Much as deep learning has been revolutionized by purpose-built optimizers that exploit properties of neural networks [19,20], this paper aims to accelerate GPs with a purpose-built method leveraging (coarse-grained) covariance matrix solves on modern hardware. We introduce an iterative method to compute gradients of the marginal log-likelihood (MLL) and the posterior mean that improves over CG in the following ways: 1) it requires \mathcal{O}(n) computation per iteration rather than CG's \mathcal{O}(n^{2}); 2) it converges rapidly and monotonically in its early stages (though it does not necessarily obtain higher precision than CG); and 3) it shows improved numerical stability in floating point arithmetic.

## Contributions.

We propose an iterative method for Gaussian process training and inference, which computes the marginal log-likelihood derivative and posterior mean via alternating projection. Each iteration of the algorithm accesses a subblock of the kernel matrix, has linear time and memory complexity, and decreases the residual near-monotonically after every epoch. We prove that the algorithm converges linearly at a rate no slower than gradient descent, despite never operating on the full kernel matrix. Empirically, our method achieves a speed-up of up to 27\times over CG-based hyperparameter training and of up to 72\times over CG-based inference on a wide range of datasets. To demonstrate its scalability and robustness to ill-conditioning, we train Gaussian processes on 4 million data points, to the best of our knowledge the largest dataset reported in the literature to-date without using inducing points or similar modeling approximations. At this scale, our method outperforms the stochastic variational Gaussian process by a significant margin.
